newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerian polls close after millions seek peace.
newsitem.headline: Algerian polls close after millions seek peace.

text.p: The curtains closed and counting started in polling stations across Algeria on Thursday after millions of Algerians, weary of bloodshed, voted in their first general election in more than five years of violence.
In heavy security deployed against possible attacks by Moslem fundamentalists -- blamed by officials for the conflict -- young and old cast ballots in what many said was a quest for peace.
Even as they voted, an Islam-oriented party contesting the poll said a bomb had seriously wounded two local election observers in a car near Djelfa in central Algiers.
"I voted for peace for me and my children," Ahmed Yanaguen, 58, told Reuters. Yanaguen and his wife, wearing a black veil, were the first to vote at El-Warda school in Telemly district.
At another city station, one young man said: "I want to contribute to finding stability and a way out of the crisis."

Voting started slowly. But by the evening of the sunlit day, with an hour to go to the scheduled close at 7 p.m. (1800 GMT), Interior Minister Mustapha Benmansour said over nine million of the 16.7 million electorate had turned out.
He announced some polling booths would stay open an hour later, until 8 p.m. (1900 GMT), to cope with the high turnout.

In the capital, where bombs early this week ripped through buses and a crowded market killing 22 people and wounding 120, men and women clutching electoral cards told Reuters they were voting for an end to the strife.
Early figures showed Algiers had one of the lowest turnouts.
Armed plainclothes police guarded polling stations, while troops and police, backed by armoured troop carriers, deployed at entrances to Algiers and in streets where rebels have attacked.
The Tribune newspaper said voters were choosing "an Assembly of hope", a phrase echoed by many voters speaking to Reuters.

Early voters included President Liamine Zeroual, dressed in a blue suit, who cast his vote in Ghazali school in Algeria's Mouradia district. He said he was "convinced the Algerian people will seize this historic opportunity and vote in large numbers".

His government says the poll is a key step towards ending the strife that began shortly after the army-backed authorities in January 1992 cancelled elections the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win.
About 60,000 people have died in the conflict.

The FIS is outlawed, but one man near a city voting station said: "Despite what they say, that the FIS has disappeared, I am not going to vote because I don't want to go back on my religious and political principles."
Frontrunners are the National Democratic Rally (RND), which groups Zeroual supporters, and the Islam-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) of Mahfoud Nahnah.

During polling, Nahnah urged the authorities to end what he termed "irregularities" against his party. He did not spell these out but MPS sources said they included the beating up of one MPS envoy at a polling booth.
Other leading parties include the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of fiercely anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
An FFS leader Seddiki Debaili also alleged irregularities which amounted to cheating. "These elections are rigged," he said.
The Interior Minister responded: "Algeria does not allow itself to permit, even by lower authorities, such irregularities. These allegations are related to political competition."
Arab League monitors, among some 200 from abroad, said the ballot was proceeding in a fair and free atmosphere.

"Our observers spread across the country have not received any complaints...I have not seen any pressure on voters and there are no doubts about the integrity of the election," their chief Kamal Said told Reuters.
Voters are casting ballots to elect a 380-member National Assembly (lower house) from more than 7,000 candidates standing for 39 political parties.

The new parliament will be Algeria's first elected multi-party assembly since independence in 1962. For nearly 30 years until the first attempt at a democratic parliamentary vote in December 1991, the oil and gas producing country was run as a one-party state by the National Liberation Front (FLN).

Because voting is under a new proportional representation system -- which virtually rules out single-party dominance -- officials are reluctant to forecast when final results will be available. Newspapers say they should be out sometime on Friday.
